headline: Apple Says It Will Charge 15% When Apps Send You Outside the App Store to Pay

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Apple makes the iPhone and the App Store, which is where people download apps like games. When someone buys something inside an app, Apple usually takes a small piece of that money as a fee. For a long time, some app makers wanted to let customers pay in other ways, like on a website, so Apple would not get that fee. A court told Apple it had to allow this. Apple did not want to lose all the money, so it said it would still charge a fee of 15% even when people pay outside the app. Smaller companies would pay less, only 5%. This has been part of a long disagreement between Apple and a game company called Epic Games, which makes the game Fortnite. Epic thinks Apple's fees are unfair and take away choices from app makers. A judge and even the Supreme Court have been involved in deciding what Apple is allowed to do. This matters because it affects how much money app makers keep, and it could also affect prices for anyone who buys things through apps.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Apple runs the App Store, where people download apps for iPhones. Normally, when someone buys something inside an app, Apple takes a cut of that money, often around 30%. For years, Epic Games, the company behind Fortnite, has argued that this is unfair and stops app makers from offering cheaper prices elsewhere. A court agreed that Apple must let apps include links that send customers to pay on a website instead of inside the app. But Apple still wanted to earn money from those outside purchases, so it tried delaying telling the court its new plan. After the Supreme Court refused to pause the case, Apple had to reveal its plan on Thursday. Apple says it will now charge a 15% fee for most apps using outside links, with lower fees for small businesses (5%) and companies in special partner programs (10%). Apple argues these fees are fair because it spends money building and maintaining the App Store's tools and technology. It also pointed out that Google charges similar or even higher fees for its own app store, Google Play, and that Epic agreed to those rates. This news matters because it shows how much control Apple has over how apps make money, and any fees companies pay often affect the prices customers see. The legal fight is not fully over, since bigger questions about whether Apple broke earlier court rules are still being decided.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Apple's App Store is the only place iPhone users can normally download apps, and Apple has long charged app developers a commission, often up to 30%, on purchases made inside those apps. Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, sued Apple years ago, arguing this system is anti-competitive because it forces developers to use Apple's payment system and blocks them from offering cheaper options elsewhere. Courts eventually ruled that Apple must allow apps to include links directing users to outside websites to complete purchases, avoiding Apple's in-app fees entirely. However, Apple has kept trying to hold onto some revenue from these outside transactions. At one point, it tried charging a 27% fee on outside purchases, which Epic argued violated the court's order. That dispute is still working its way through the legal system, with questions about whether Apple was in 'contempt,' meaning it disobeyed a judge's order. While that bigger issue awaits a possible Supreme Court decision, a separate court asked Apple to reveal what commission structure it planned to use going forward. Apple tried to delay this by asking to pause the case until the Supreme Court ruled, but the request was denied. As a result, Apple submitted its proposal this week: a 15% commission for most apps using outside payment links, 5% for small businesses, and 10% for developers in special partner programs, such as those distributing video, news, or mini-apps, as well as for subscription renewals. Apple defends these rates by comparing them to Google's Play Store, which charges similarly, and by explaining that it needs the money to support the technology and services behind the App Store. This case matters beyond just Apple and Epic. It could shape how much money software developers of all sizes keep from their sales, which can affect the prices and features offered to everyday users. It also raises broader questions about how much power giant tech companies should have over the online marketplaces they control, and how courts can enforce fairness in a fast-changing digital economy.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: For years, Apple has controlled how developers get paid for purchases made inside apps on iPhones, typically charging commissions as high as 30% through its own in-app payment system. Epic Games, creator of the wildly popular game Fortnite, challenged this system in a lawsuit, arguing that Apple's rules were anti-competitive because they prevented developers from directing customers to cheaper payment options outside the App Store. After a lengthy legal battle, courts ruled that Apple must allow developers to include links inside their apps that send users to external websites to complete purchases, bypassing Apple's commission structure altogether. Yet Apple has continued trying to preserve some financial benefit from these transactions. In one instance, it attempted to impose a 27% fee on purchases made through these external links, along with restrictions on how those links could be displayed to users. Epic argued this amounted to Apple defying the original court order, and the matter of whether Apple was in contempt of court is still unresolved, potentially headed to the U.S. Supreme Court. While that larger question loomed, a lower court in California ordered Apple to formally lay out what commission rates it intended to charge going forward. Apple attempted to delay this disclosure, asking the court to pause proceedings until the Supreme Court weighed in on the contempt issue. This week, the Supreme Court rejected that request, forcing Apple's hand. In its new filing, Apple proposed a tiered commission system: 15% for standard apps using external payment links, a reduced 5% for small businesses, and 10% for developers enrolled in special partner programs covering video, news, and mini-apps, as well as for subscription renewals. Apple defended these numbers by pointing to its ongoing investment in the App Store's infrastructure, security systems, and developer tools, arguing it deserves compensation for the platform it built and maintains. The company also drew a comparison to Google, whose Play Store charges 20% for standard link-out purchases and 10% for subscription renewals, noting that Epic itself had accepted those terms in a separate settlement. This ongoing dispute has significance far beyond two companies feuding in court. It touches on how much authority tech giants like Apple should have over the digital marketplaces they built, and how that authority affects smaller developers who rely on these platforms to reach customers. The outcome could influence app prices, the variety of payment options available to consumers, and how strictly courts hold powerful companies accountable when they are found to violate antitrust rulings. It's a case study in the tension between corporate control over technology ecosystems and calls for fairer competition online.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Apple's App Store has long operated as a walled garden: to publish an app on iPhones, developers typically had to use Apple's in-app payment system and pay Apple a commission, often as high as 30%, on digital purchases. This arrangement became the center of a prolonged antitrust battle with Epic Games, the studio behind Fortnite, which argued that Apple's restrictions unfairly limited competition by preventing developers from offering customers cheaper alternatives to pay outside the app. A federal court ultimately ruled that Apple must permit developers to include links within their apps directing users to external websites where they could complete purchases without going through Apple's payment system, and therefore without paying Apple's usual commission. Rather than accepting this fully, Apple attempted to preserve revenue from these external transactions by imposing a new 27% fee on purchases made through these outside links, along with rules limiting how developers could present those links to users. Epic contended that this maneuver effectively violated the spirit, if not the letter, of the earlier court order, raising the question of whether Apple was in contempt of court, a legal finding that a party has willfully disobeyed a judicial ruling. That contempt question remains unresolved and may eventually reach the U.S. Supreme Court. In the meantime, a district court in Northern California demanded that Apple disclose, in more concrete terms, what commission structure it intended to apply going forward. Apple sought to delay this disclosure, asking the courts to pause proceedings until the Supreme Court addressed the contempt issue first. This week, the Supreme Court declined to grant that pause, compelling Apple to submit its proposal. The plan calls for a 15% commission on standard apps using external payment links, with reduced rates for smaller players: 5% for small businesses, and 10% for developers enrolled in Apple's specialized partner programs covering video, news, and mini-apps, as well as for subscription renewals. Apple has defended these figures as reasonable compensation for the technological infrastructure, security systems, and developer tools it maintains to support its ecosystem. It also drew a comparison to Google's Play Store, which imposes a 20% commission on standard external link purchases, 15% for special program participants, and 10% for subscription renewals, noting that Epic Games had already agreed to comparable terms with Google in a separate settlement. This dispute carries implications well beyond the immediate conflict between Apple and Epic. It highlights broader tensions in the tech industry over how much control dominant platform owners should retain over commerce that occurs through the ecosystems they build, even after regulators or courts intervene to encourage competition. For everyday consumers, the outcome could influence app pricing, the availability of alternative payment methods, and the overall cost of digital goods and subscriptions. For developers, especially smaller companies with tighter margins, these commission rates can determine whether external payment options are actually financially worthwhile to implement. More broadly, the case illustrates the ongoing challenge courts face in enforcing antitrust rulings against powerful technology companies capable of adapting their business practices in ways that technically comply with legal mandates while still preserving much of their original revenue streams.

questions: If you made an app, do you think it would be fair for a company like Apple to take a cut of your sales just because your app is downloaded from their store? Why or why not?
How might these kinds of fees affect the price you pay for apps, in-app purchases, or subscriptions on your own phone or tablet?
Why do you think it's important for courts to be involved in deciding how much big tech companies can charge, and what could happen if no one checked their power?
